title: Explaining Constraints: Budget, Time & Scope
titleEs: Explicar las limitaciones: presupuesto, plazo y alcance
summary: Explain why something cannot be done without sounding defensive: name the constraint precisely (time, budget, scope), give the reason with *given (that)*, and use a first look at the **mixed conditional** (*If we had tested in April, we would have more options now*) to link a past decision to the situation today and take your share of responsibility.
canDo: Name a time, budget or scope constraint precisely and neutrally (*we're up against…*, *the budget doesn't stretch to…*, *it's out of scope*).
Give reasons with *given (that)* and say what a change would require (*a change request*).
Link an unreal past to its effect now with a mixed conditional: *if* + past perfect, *would* + bare infinitive + *now*.
Tell *'d = had* from *'d = would* by ear, and say *than*, *and* and *scope* without extra vowels.

focus.grammar: Preview of mixed conditionals: If + had + past participle, … would + bare infinitive (now) · contrast with the Second and Third Conditionals · 'd = had / would · given + noun / given that + clause · it would need + noun
focus.lexis: be up against (a deadline), the budget doesn't stretch to, fixed-price, in scope / out of scope, a change request, be tied to, squeeze something in, given (that), it comes down to, realistically, that's on us
focus.afh: weak forms: had → 'd (if we'd known), than /ðən/, and /ənd/ · 'd = had or would, by context · scope /skoʊp/ without an e · FEAsible with a long /iː/ and /z/ · budget /ˈbʌdʒ.ɪt/

warmup: Think of something you wanted to do at work or in your studies but couldn't. Was the obstacle time, money or the limits of the job? How did you explain it, and did the other person accept the explanation?

scenario.title: Why not just add servers?
scenario.context: Helen has asked Ryan a simple question: couldn't more servers fix the search? Ryan answers in writing before their call.
scenario.speaker: ryan
scenario.text: Hi Helen, thanks for asking; here's the short version. Time: {{we're up against}} go-live in three weeks, and a proper fix to the indexing would take about five. Budget: the contract is {{fixed-price}}, so extra servers would come out of your budget, and the test suggests they wouldn't solve the problem anyway. Scope: the search was {{in scope}}, but rebuilding the indexing wasn't, so it {{would need a change request}}. Looking back, {{if we had tested}} at full scale in April, we {{would have}} more options now. {{Given}} where we are, we'll come back to you on Friday with the options. Ryan

discovery.intro: Two sentences Ryan says to Helen. Both talk about things that are not true. The question is: when?
discovery.speaker: ryan
discovery.text: {{If we had tested}} at full scale in April, we {{would have}} more options now. We didn't, so today the choice is narrower. And {{if the indexing weren't}} the problem, extra servers {{would solve}} it in a week. But it is, so they won't.

organizer.title: Two times in one sentence
organizer.prompt: Place each half of Ryan's first sentence on the time line. Copy the words from the text.

points.text: We didn't test at full scale.

points.gap: if we had tested at full scale
accept: if we had tested at full scale
if we'd tested at full scale
if we had tested at full scale in april

points.gap: we would have more options now

organizer.explain: A mixed conditional joins an unreal past (*had* + past participle) with an unreal present (*would* + bare infinitive): a past that did not happen, and the present it would have created.

questions.q: In *If we had tested at full scale in April, we would have more options now*: did the team test in April? Do they have more options now? Which half talks about the past and which about the present?
questions.model: No, they did not test at full scale in April, and no, they do not have more options now: both halves are unreal. The *if*-half imagines a different past (April); the main half describes the present result of that imagined past (*now*). That is why the times are mixed: the sentence links a past cause to a present situation. In a Third Conditional both halves would be past (*we would have had more options in May*).
criteria: You said both halves are unreal: they didn't test, and they don't have more options.
You said the *if*-half is about the past (April) and the main half about the present (now).
You said the sentence links a past cause to a present result.

questions.q: Write the pattern of each half of *If we had tested… / we would have more options now*. Then compare *if the indexing weren't the problem, extra servers would solve it*. What changes in the *if*-half, and what stays the same in the main half? And what does *'d* mean in *if we'd spotted* and in *we'd have*?
questions.model: Mixed conditional (past → present): *if* + past perfect (*had tested*), then *would* + bare infinitive (*would have*, where *have* is the main verb: *have more options*). The second sentence is a Second Conditional: *if* + past simple (*weren't*), *would* + bare infinitive. The main half is the same in both (*would* + infinitive = unreal present); the *if*-half changes: past perfect for an unreal past, past simple for an unreal present. *'d* is *had* in *if we'd spotted* (a past participle follows) and *would* in *we'd have* (a bare infinitive follows).
criteria: You wrote *if* + past perfect, *would* + bare infinitive for the mixed conditional.
You said the Second Conditional uses *if* + past simple, with the same main half.
You said *'d* = *had* before a past participle and *would* before a bare infinitive.

questions.q: Ryan tells Helen: *If we had tested at full scale in April, we would be in a different position today. That's on us.* Why does he say *we* and not *the supplier* or *Oliver*? What does this add to the list of constraints (time, budget, scope)?

signals.label: constraints alone can sound like excuses

questions.model: With *we* and *that's on us*, Ryan takes responsibility for the team instead of blaming a supplier or a colleague. The mixed conditional explains how the present constraint was created, without excuses: it names a past decision and its effect today. A list of constraints alone (budget, time, scope) can sound like a wall or a set of excuses; owning the team's part makes Ryan sound honest, so Helen is more likely to trust the options he brings on Friday.
criteria: You said *we* and *that's on us* take responsibility instead of blaming others.
You said the conditional explains the origin of the constraint without sounding like an excuse.
You linked this honesty to trust in what Ryan proposes next.

points: Name each constraint precisely and neutrally: time (*we're up against go-live*), budget (*the budget doesn't stretch to…*), scope (*it's out of scope, so it would need a change request*). Give the reason with *given (that)*.
**Preview:** a mixed conditional links an unreal past to its effect now: *if* + past perfect, *would* + bare infinitive (+ *now / today*). You will study mixed conditionals in depth in B2.2.
Compare: Second Conditional = unreal present (*if the indexing weren't the problem, servers would solve it*); Third = unreal past with a past result (*we would have had more options in May*).
*'d* can be *had* or *would*: before a past participle it is *had* (*if we'd spotted*); before a bare infinitive it is *would* (*we'd have more room*).
formulas: If + had + past participle, … would + bare infinitive (+ now / today)
given + noun phrase · given that + clause
… is out of scope, so it would need a change request
rule.note: Spanish mixes times in the same way (*si hubiéramos probado en abril, ahora tendríamos más opciones*), so the logic is familiar. The typical error is putting *would* in the *if*-half: *if we would have tested*. The *if*-half never takes *would*.

discovery.tts: If we [had](/həd/) tested [at](/ət/) full scale in April, we [would](/wəd/) have more options now. We didn't, so today the choice is narrower. [And](/ənd/) if the indexing weren't the problem, extra servers [would](/wəd/) solve it in a week. [But](/bət/) it is, so they won't.

phonetics.intro: Al explicar limitaciones, las frases se llenan de palabras funcionales que el nativo reduce: *had* se convierte en *'d*, *than* en «dhən» y *and* en «ənd». Si las pronuncias plenas, suenas lento y enfático, como si discutieras. Y hay un reto de comprensión: *'d* suena igual para *had* y para *would*; lo que viene detrás te dice cuál es.

items.meaning: if we had known (an unreal past)

alerts.text: *Had* auxiliar se reduce a /həd/ o, más a menudo, a *'d* /d/: *if we'd known* «if-uid-NOUN». No «if-ui-JAD-noun» con *had* plena.
*'d* suena igual para *had* y para *would*. La pista es lo que sigue: participio (*known, tested*) = *had*; infinitivo (*be, have*) = *would*. Compara las dos variantes.
*We'd known*: la d se une a la n sin vocal en medio: «uid-NOUN», no «ui-de-NOUN».

example.speaker: helen
example.text: If we'd known in April, we'd be in a different position now.

alerts.text: *Than* es /ðən/: «dhən», con schwa. La forma plena /ðæn/ solo aparece si se enfatiza.
/ð/ es sonora: la lengua entre los dientes, vibrando, como la d suave de «nada». No «dan» ni «zan».
No confundas *than* (comparación) con *then* (luego): en habla rápida, *than* suena «dhən» y *then*, «dhen». *Longer* lleva g: «LÓN-guer».

example.speaker: oliver
example.text: A proper fix would take longer than we have.
example.tts: A proper fix [would](/wəd/) take longer than we have.

items.meaning: the two most common limits on a project

alerts.text: *And* es /ənd/ o /ən/: «ənd», casi «n», unido a la palabra anterior: «TAI-mənd». No «AND» con a plena.
*Budget*: /ʌ/ en la primera sílaba, «BA» breve; la segunda es una /ɪ/ débil: «BÁ-dyit». No «bud-YET».
*dg* es /dʒ/, «dy» como en «yo» dicho con fuerza: «BÁ-dyit».

example.speaker: ryan
example.text: It comes down to time and budget, not effort.
example.tts: It comes down to time [and](/ənd/) budget, not effort.

items.meaning: the range of work that has been agreed

alerts.text: Empieza con /sk/: «SKOUP», sin e delante. Nada de «es-KOUP».
US /oʊ/, «ou»; UK /əʊ/, «əu»: un diptongo, no una o pura.
*Out of scope*: la t de *out* se une a *of*: «au-rəv-SKOUP» (US), «au-təv-SKƏUP» (UK).

example.speaker: alex
example.text: Rebuilding the indexing is out of scope, so it would need a change request.
example.tts: Rebuilding the indexing is [out](/ˈWɾ/) [of](/əv/) scope, so it [would](/wəd/) need a change request.

alerts.text: La s suena /z/, sonora, con zumbido, como en *zoo*: «FII-zə-bəl».
Acento en la primera sílaba, FII; *-ble* es /bəl/, sin vocal plena. No «fea-SI-ble».

l1.title: Would in the if-half
l1.text: The *if*-half never takes *would*. For an unreal past, use the past perfect.
l1.wrong: If we would have tested in April, we would have more options now.
l1.right: If we had tested in April, we would have more options now.

l1.title: Will in the result
l1.text: Both halves are unreal, so the result takes *would*, not *will*: the extra options do not exist.
l1.wrong: If we had tested in April, we will have more options now.
l1.right: If we had tested in April, we would have more options now.

l1.title: Realize for «realizar»
l1.text: *Realize* means to understand suddenly. For work, use *carry out*, *do* or *complete*.
l1.wrong: We can't realize the rebuild in three weeks.
l1.right: We can't carry out the rebuild in three weeks.

l1.title: Actual for «actual»
l1.text: *Actual* means real. For the one that exists now, use *current*.
l1.wrong: The actual budget doesn't stretch to extra servers.
l1.right: The current budget doesn't stretch to extra servers.

l1.title: Economic for «económico»
l1.text: *Economic* is about the economy of a country. For money in a project, use *financial* or *budget*; for cheap, *inexpensive*.
l1.wrong: We have economic limits on this project.
l1.right: We have budget constraints on this project.

task.title: Explaining why it can't be done
task.scenario: Help-center project, ten days before launch. Laura, the head of support, wants video tutorials in the help center at launch, and she isn't happy that the answer is no. Good videos take about a month to produce; there is no money for video in this phase, and videos were not in the agreed scope. Nobody asked about videos when the scope was agreed in March. Record a voice message for Laura that explains the constraints, takes your share of responsibility and suggests a way forward.
task.brief: Explain time, budget and scope constraints neutrally, and use a mixed conditional to link a past decision to the situation now.
steps: Show you understand why Laura wants the videos.
Time: the launch date against the production time, with numbers.
Budget and scope: what isn't covered and what a change would need.
A mixed conditional about March and now, and your share of responsibility.
A realistic way forward and a date to talk.

chunks.label: responsibility
chunks.re: \bthat's on us\b|\bthat is on us\b|\bour (responsibility|fault|mistake)\b|\bwe should have\b

extra.title: Extra: the formal note for the steering committee
extra.brief: Write one or two formal sentences: the scope constraint with *given that*, what a change would require, and a proposal for the second phase.
keywords: were not included in the agreed scope
would require a formal change request

parts.speaker: alex
parts.text: Hi Laura, it's Alex, about the video tutorials. {{I understand why}} your team wants them, so here's where we are. Time: {{we're up against}} the launch in ten days, and good videos take about a month to make. Budget: video production isn't in this phase, and {{the budget doesn't stretch to}} an agency. Scope: videos weren't in the agreed scope, so they would need {{a change request}}. To be honest, {{if we had talked}} about videos in March, {{we would have}} them ready {{now}}. Nobody raised it, and {{that's on us}} as much as anyone. {{Given}} where we are, could we plan three short videos for {{phase two}}? Let's talk on Thursday.
parts.label: Voice message to an unhappy stakeholder (neutral)
notes: *I understand why your team wants them*: empathy before the constraints, so the no is not a wall.
Time, Budget, Scope as three labelled points, each with one fact: *ten days* against *a month*; *isn't in this phase*; *weren't in the agreed scope*.
*If we had talked about videos in March, we would have them ready now*: a mixed conditional; the past that did not happen and the present it would have created.
*That's on us as much as anyone*: Alex shares the responsibility instead of blaming the support team.
*Given where we are, could we plan… for phase two? Let's talk on Thursday*: a realistic way forward and a date.
parts.tts: Hi Laura, it's Alex, about the video tutorials. I understand why your team wants them, so here's where we are. Time: we're up against the launch in ten days, [and](/ənd/) good videos take about a month to make. Budget: video production isn't in this phase, [and](/ənd/) the budget doesn't stretch to an agency. Scope: videos weren't in the agreed scope, so they [would](/wəd/) need a change request. To be honest, if we [had](/həd/) talked about videos in March, we [would](/wəd/) have them ready now. Nobody raised it, [and](/ənd/) that's on us [as](/əz/) much [as](/əz/) anyone. Given where we are, [could](/kəd/) we plan three short videos [for](/fəɹ/) phase two? Let's talk on Thursday.

parts.speaker: emma
parts.text: {{Given that}} video tutorials {{were not included in the agreed scope}}, their production {{would require a formal change request}}; {{we would therefore propose}} to include them in the second phase.
parts.label: One formal sentence for the committee
notes: *Given that* + clause: the constraint as a neutral fact.
*Would require a formal change request*: the formal consequence, in the conditional.
*We would therefore propose*: a formal, softened proposal.
parts.tts: Given that video tutorials were not included in the agreed scope, their production [would](/wəd/) require a formal change request; we [would](/wəd/) therefore propose to include them in the second phase.

selfCheck.text: Si Laura escucha tu mensaje, ¿siente que la entiendes o que le pones un muro de excusas? ¿Qué frase reconoce su punto de vista y cuál reconoce tu parte de responsabilidad?
¿Nombraste las limitaciones con frases neutras (*we're up against*, *the budget doesn't stretch to*) y no con chat (*no way*, *maxed out*) ni con frases de culpa (*your team never asked*)?
¿Tu condicional mixto tiene *if* + *had* + participio y *would* + infinitivo sin *have* + participio (*we would have them ready now*)? ¿Ningún *would* en la parte del *if*?
¿Dijiste *realize* por «realizar», *actual* por «actual» o *economic* por «económico»? Debe ser *carry out / do*, *current* y *budget / financial*.

Escúchate: ¿dijiste *had* y *would* en forma débil (*if we'd talked*, *we'd have*)? Si te faltó una palabra (*change request*), ¿la explicaste con otras (*a formal request to change what we agreed*) sin detenerte?
